intro: A newspaper drops one comma from a writer's thank-you note and turns her parents into a professor and a library. A hiring manager reads a cover letter that promises attention to detail and stops at the word you're. Neither reader needed a grammar book to react. Each one read a small mark or a small word as a signal about the person behind the page, and each decided, in about two seconds, how much to trust what came next.

This unit is about those signals at full strength. The first chapter takes the marks most students avoid and shows what each one does: the semicolon that joins equals, the colon that points forward, the dash that raises its voice and the parentheses that lower it, the comma that follows structure rather than breath, the hyphen that keeps a small-business owner from being a short one, and the brackets and ellipses that keep a quotation honest. You will also see how professional editors decide when two rulebooks disagree.

The second chapter steps back and asks where rules come from and what they are for. You will learn the difference between describing a language and prescribing it, meet rules that quietly died and one pronoun that the major guides accepted within three years, and practice the registers of email, applications and cover letters. You will build a ten-minute editing routine, learn which reference settles which question, and think carefully about the many Englishes of Chicago and about the plain respect of calling people what they call themselves.
bigQuestion: When the rules of punctuation and usage disagree with each other, or change under our feet, how does a writer decide what a reader needs?

timeline.t: The Venetian printer Aldus Manutius uses the first semicolon in a printed book; the mark spreads across Europe.
Samuel Johnson's Dictionary of the English Language fixes spellings and meanings that English writers still follow.
The Declaration of Independence lists Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness with no serial comma.
Noah Webster's American Dictionary sets American spellings such as color and center apart from British ones.
Henry Alford's A Plea for the Queen's English condemns the split infinitive, launching a rule that lasts a century.
The University of Chicago Press publishes the first Chicago Manual of Style, still the guide of most book publishers.
The Associated Press issues its first stylebook so that newspapers across the country punctuate the same way.
Webster's Third New International Dictionary records usage as it is, and critics accuse it of abandoning standards.
College writing teachers adopt the resolution Students' Right to Their Own Language, affirming every dialect's grammar.
A federal appeals court reads a missing comma in a Maine overtime law in favor of delivery drivers; AP and Chicago accept singular they.
The APA manual endorses singular they in all writing, and Merriam-Webster names they its Word of the Year.
You punctuate a long sentence by its structure, write a cover letter with zero errors, and settle a usage dispute with a reference.

words.d: a group of words with a subject and a verb that can stand alone as a sentence
the error of joining two complete sentences with only a comma
the long dash that sets off an interruption or throws emphasis on what follows
describing a clause that adds information without narrowing the meaning; set off by commas
the comma before and or or in a list of three or more items; required by some guides, dropped by others
two or more words working as one adjective before a noun, usually joined by a hyphen
three spaced periods marking words removed from a quotation
an editor's or writer's running list of decisions made for one manuscript
stating rules about what writers and speakers should do
recording what speakers and writers actually do
the level of formality and word choices matched to the reader and the occasion
a large searchable collection of real published writing used to study usage

test.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
choices: The snow stopped; the plows went out.
The snow stopped; which let the plows out.
Because the snow stopped; the plows went out.
test.why: A semicolon joins two independent clauses; only the first choice has a complete sentence on each side.

test.q: What must come before a colon that introduces a list?
test.why: The words before a colon must be able to stand alone; 'The reasons are:' fails that test.

test.q: Which mark joins a range such as pages 12 to 18?
test.why: The en dash, about as wide as an N, marks ranges and pairs; the hyphen joins words and the em dash interrupts.

test.q: Compared with commas and dashes, what do parentheses do to an interruption?
test.why: The unit describes three volumes: commas are neutral, dashes are loud, parentheses whisper.

test.q: A writer quotes a sentence but replaces the word 'she' with the person's name. How must the name appear?
test.why: Brackets signal that the words inside are the writer's, not the source's.

test.q: What is the difference between 'The players who were late ran laps' and 'The players, who were late, ran laps'?
choices: The second is a comma splice
The first means only the late players ran; the second means all of them ran
test.why: Commas mark a nonrestrictive clause that adds information; without them the clause narrows which players.

test.q: Which guide generally leaves out the serial comma?
test.why: AP style drops the comma before the last item unless a list would confuse; the others require it.
A compound modifier before a noun takes a hyphen; adverbs ending in -ly do not, and numbers like twenty-five do.

test.q: In American style, where does a period go when a quotation ends a sentence and no citation follows?
test.why: Periods and commas go inside the closing quotation mark; the period moves only when a parenthetical citation follows.

test.q: How should the title of a novel appear in an essay, and how should a short story's title appear?
choices: Novel in quotation marks, story in italics
Novel in italics, story in quotation marks
test.why: Standalone works take italics; parts of larger works take quotation marks.

test.q: Which statement is descriptive rather than prescriptive?
choices: Always use fewer with countable nouns.
Most speakers say 'less' with countable nouns in casual speech.
test.why: A descriptive statement reports what speakers do; the others tell writers what they should do.

test.q: What did the major style guides do about singular they between 2017 and 2019?
choices: Accepted it, with the APA endorsing it in all writing
test.why: AP and Chicago accepted limited use in 2017, and the APA manual's seventh edition endorsed it in 2019.

test.q: Which cover-letter sentence follows the unit's advice about evidence?
choices: I am a hard worker with great attention to detail.
I would be an asset to you're team.
I have many skills that would help your company.
On one job I caught a three-quarter-inch error on a header before the wall went up.
test.why: A cover letter backs each claim with a specific detail rather than a vague label.

test.q: In the ten-minute edit, which pass comes first?
choices: Checking meaning by reading the first sentence of each paragraph
Searching for your personal error list
test.why: Meaning comes first because a paragraph doing the wrong job costs more than any mechanical error.

test.q: How does the unit describe African American English?
choices: A variety with consistent grammar, studied for decades
A register used only in email
test.why: Linguists established that it is a full system with rules of its own; Standard English is one variety among many.

write.prompt: A school board proposes a rule that every graded assignment in the district must follow one style guide for punctuation and usage, with points taken off for every departure. Argue for or against the rule, using evidence from both chapters about how rules differ, how they change, and what readers actually need.
tips: Claim: take a clear position on the rule, or propose a specific change to it, in one sentence.
Evidence: use at least three cases from the unit, such as the two publishers' comma rules, the Maine overtime case, the guides' shift on singular they, or the ferry sentence punctuated by structure.
Reasoning: explain what each case shows about the purpose of a rule, which is that a reader should never have to read a sentence twice.
The other side: name the strongest argument for the opposite position, such as consistency or fairness in grading, and answer it directly.
Register: write for a school board in a formal register, and proofread in passes before you turn it in.
